title: ITD 256 Final Exam Review
description: Built from the highlighted portions of the instructor's course review: database and file-system basics, the DBMS and data models, keys and integrity, normalization, SQL, transactions, and data warehousing, NoSQL and connectivity.

questions.question: Match each basic term to its definition.

pairs.right: Raw facts, such as a telephone number or a birth date, with little meaning unless organized
A character or group of characters with a specific meaning, used to define and store data (also called an attribute)
A logically connected set of fields that describes a person, place or thing (also called an entity instance)
A collection of related records (also called an entity)

questions.question: A record in a file system corresponds to which database term?
options: An entity instance (a row)
An attribute
An entity (a table)
A constraint
questions.explanation: A record is a set of related fields describing one person, place or thing, which in a table is a row. A field is an attribute, and a table is an entity.

questions.question: A field is also known as a(n):
options: Entity instance
Attribute
Entity
Record
questions.explanation: Field = attribute, record = entity instance, table = entity.

questions.question: Data that exists in its original (raw) state is called:
options: Structured data
Semistructured data
Unstructured data
Metadata
questions.explanation: Structured data results from formatting the raw data; semistructured data (such as XML) is only partially processed.

questions.question: Data that has been formatted to fit a defined structure is called:
options: Unstructured data
Raw data
Redundant data
Structured data
questions.explanation: Structure is applied depending on the type of processing the data will go through.

questions.question: What is a cloud database?
options: A database created and maintained with cloud services that provide defined performance measures
A database stored on a single local server
A database that can only be queried by OLAP tools
A backup copy kept off-site
questions.explanation: A cloud database can behave like a centralized or distributed one, but the provider (AWS, Azure, Google Cloud) deals with the infrastructure.

questions.question: What is an analytical database?
options: A database that processes day-to-day transactions
A database that stores historical data and business metrics used exclusively for tactical or strategic decision making
A database with no tables
A database that stores only images
questions.explanation: Analytical databases serve decision making, not day-to-day operations.

questions.question: What is a data warehouse?
options: A backup of every table in a transactional database
A file system of spreadsheets
A database that stores data in a format optimized for decision support
A tool for entering data faster
questions.explanation: Operational data is optimized for updates; warehouse data is optimized for reading and analysis.

questions.question: Why is database design important?
options: Design only affects how the screens look
Good design makes a DBMS unnecessary
Design matters only for very small databases
A well-designed database makes data management easier and produces accurate, valuable information; a poor design causes difficult-to-trace errors
questions.explanation: A poorly designed database can cause errors that lead to poor decision making.

questions.question: Using Microsoft Excel as a database is an appropriate use of a spreadsheet.
questions.explanation: It is a classic misuse: spreadsheets lack the integrity, security, multi-user control and relationships that a DBMS provides.

questions.question: Match each problem to the file-system limitation it illustrates.

pairs.right: Every new report needs extensive custom programming
Ad hoc queries are hard; there is no query language

pairs.left: Lack of security and limited data sharing
pairs.right: Left up to each developer
Few if any standards

questions.explanation: These are some of the problems with file system data processing.

questions.question: What is data dependence?
options: A change in how the data is stored forces a change in how it is accessed
Data that can only be read by one user
Data that depends on other data for its meaning
Data copied into several places
questions.explanation: With data dependence, programs must be modified when the storage characteristics change.

questions.question: What is data independence?
options: Data that is independent of any business rules
Data storage characteristics can change without affecting the programs' ability to access the data
Data stored in more than one table
Data that can never be changed
questions.explanation: Its practical significance is the difference between the logical format (what the user or application sees) and the physical format (how it is stored on hardware, which should be hidden entirely).

questions.question: Which statement about the logical and physical formats of data is correct?
options: Logical is the actual storage on hardware; physical is the user's view
They are two names for the same thing
Logical is the representation presented to the application or user; physical is the actual storage on hardware and should be hidden from the user
Physical is the representation presented to the user
questions.explanation: Data independence lets the physical format change without the logical view being affected.

questions.question: What is data redundancy?
options: Storing data in an encrypted form
Keeping a backup copy of the database
Storing data in more than one table
Unnecessarily storing the same data in different places
questions.explanation: Redundancy produces islands of information and raises the probability of different versions of the same data.

questions.question: Anomalies develop when:
options: Not all of the required changes to redundant data are made successfully
A table has no primary key
A query returns no rows
Users enter data too quickly
questions.explanation: Types are update anomalies (inconsistent data), insertion anomalies (incomplete new data) and deletion anomalies (partial removal).

questions.question: Match each anomaly to its description.

pairs.right: A change made in only some places leaves the data inconsistent
New data cannot be added completely
Removing a row also removes other, still-needed data

questions.question: Compared with a file system, a database system allows for:
options: Less security but faster development
More data independence, more robust organization and better control of data access
More redundancy but simpler design
No need for a data dictionary
questions.explanation: These are the advantages of a database over file-based storage.

questions.question: A database system is best described as:
options: Only the software that stores data
A single computer running a database
An organization of components that define and regulate the collection, storage, management and use of data within a database environment
A collection of spreadsheets
questions.explanation: The components are hardware, software, people, procedures and data.

questions.question: Which are the five components of a database system environment?
options: Tables, rows, columns, keys and indexes
Entities, attributes, relationships, constraints and rules
Servers, clients, networks, files and backups
Hardware, software, people, procedures and data
questions.explanation: A database system is more than the DBMS software.

questions.question: What does the data dictionary store?
options: The definitions of data elements and their relationships
Only the user passwords
A copy of every row in the database
The SQL statements users have run
questions.explanation: Data dictionary management is one of the DBMS functions.

questions.question: Which DBMS function enables recovery of the database after a failure?
options: Security management
Backup and recovery management
Data transformation and presentation
Multiuser access control
questions.explanation: Backup and recovery lets you restore the database after a failure.

questions.question: Which DBMS function minimizes redundancy and maximizes consistency?
options: Data storage management
Backup and recovery management
Data integrity management
Database communication interfaces
questions.explanation: Integrity management is what keeps the data consistent.

questions.question: What is a query language?
options: A language in which users write each step of the retrieval procedure
A language for designing screens
A language only for creating tables
A language in which users specify what result they want, and the system determines how to produce it
questions.explanation: This is why SQL is called a nonprocedural language.

questions.question: What does SQL stand for? (Four words, e.g. Structured ___ ___ ___)
questions.explanation: SQL is the de facto query language and data access standard, supported by nearly all DBMS vendors with slight variations.

questions.question: What is a data model?
options: A simple representation of complex real-world data structures, useful for supporting a specific problem domain
The finished database filled with data
A backup of the data dictionary
The physical files on a server
questions.explanation: Data modeling is creating a specific data model for a determined problem domain.

questions.question: Which are the three levels of data modeling?
options: Primary, secondary and tertiary
Conceptual, logical and physical
Entity, attribute and relationship
Structured, semistructured and unstructured
questions.explanation: Conceptual (big-picture entities and relationships), logical (tables, keys and attributes, independent of the physical details) and physical (how it is stored in a particular DBMS).

questions.question: Match each data model building block to its definition.

pairs.right: A person, place, thing or event
A characteristic of an entity
An association among entities
A restriction placed on the data

questions.question: What do business rules help to identify?
options: Only the primary keys
Only the SQL queries needed
Entities, attributes, relationships and constraints
The hardware to buy
questions.explanation: Nouns in business rules translate into entities and verbs into relationships.

questions.question: Relationships are always bidirectional.
questions.explanation: To identify a relationship's type, ask both: how many B are related to one A, and how many A are related to one B?

questions.question: In the relational model, a relation is:
options: A link between two databases
A foreign key
A SQL query
A table, a matrix of intersecting rows (tuples) and columns (attributes)
questions.explanation: Rows are tuples and columns are attributes.

questions.question: An RDBMS does which of the following?
options: Hides the complexities of the relational model from the user, making it easier to understand and implement
Requires users to write the physical access paths
Stores data only in hierarchies
Replaces the need for keys
questions.explanation: The RDBMS performs the basic functions of the hierarchical and network DBMS systems, too.

questions.question: What is an entity relationship diagram (ERD)?
options: A list of all SQL statements
A graphical representation of the entities and relationships in a database structure
A table of data types
A list of users and permissions
questions.explanation: ERDs use graphic representations to model database components.

questions.question: Match each ER-model term to its meaning.

pairs.right: A row in a relational table
Describe particular characteristics of an entity
The term used to label relationship types (1:1, 1:M, M:N)

questions.question: Match each object-oriented term to its relational equivalent.

pairs.right: A row
A table
A subclass takes on the methods and attributes of its parent classes (no relational equivalent)

questions.question: In the object-oriented data model, what is inheritance?
options: Copying a table into another database
A foreign key referencing a parent table
An object inherits the methods and attributes of its parent classes
Deleting a parent row deletes its children
questions.explanation: A class hierarchy resembles an upside-down tree in which each class has only one parent.

questions.question: Which of these is an advantage of the relational model?
options: It needs very little hardware
It requires no keys
It eliminates the need for design
It isolates the end user from physical-level details and promotes structural independence
questions.explanation: Other advantages: tabular view improves conceptual simplicity, ad hoc querying with SQL, relationships done through primary and foreign keys. A disadvantage is that it needs substantial hardware and system software overhead.

questions.question: Which of the following describes the logical model, as opposed to the physical model?
options: The logical model represents the data as the user or application sees it (tables, keys, relationships) and is independent of storage details
The logical model describes where each file is on disk
The logical model is the same as the data dictionary
The logical model is built after the physical model
questions.explanation: The physical model describes how the data is actually stored on hardware.

questions.question: What is a key?
options: Any attribute that cannot be null
One or more attributes that determine other attributes
A password to the database
A column holding only numbers
questions.explanation: Keys ensure each row is uniquely identifiable, establish relationships among tables and ensure data integrity.

questions.question: What is a primary key?
options: Any column used in a WHERE clause
The first column of a table
An attribute or combination of attributes that uniquely identifies a row
An attribute that may be null
questions.explanation: Each table row must have a primary key.

questions.question: What is a natural key?
options: A key generated automatically by the DBMS
A foreign key that matches exactly one row
A key made of two or more attributes
A real-world identifier that uniquely identifies real-world objects, familiar to end users
questions.explanation: A natural key can be used as the primary key of the entity being modeled.

questions.question: What is a surrogate key?
options: An artificial (made-up) primary key, such as an auto-number
A key that references another table
A key taken from a real-world identifier
A key that is allowed to be null
questions.explanation: Surrogate means 'in place of'.

questions.question: When are surrogate primary keys useful?
options: Whenever a table has fewer than ten rows
When no natural key is suitable, when the primary key would be a composite of several data types, or when the natural key is too long to be usable
Only when the table has a foreign key
Never; natural keys should always be used
questions.explanation: These are the three situations listed.

questions.question: What is a composite key?
options: A key made up of one text and one number
A key shared by two tables
A key made up of multiple attributes
A key that has been encrypted
questions.explanation: Each attribute that is part of the key is a key attribute.

questions.question: What is a foreign key?
options: A key that points to a table in a different database
A key that is not allowed to match anything
An artificial key
The primary key of one table placed in another table to create a common attribute
questions.explanation: Foreign keys are how independent tables are linked.

questions.question: What is entity integrity?
options: The condition in which each row in a table has its own unique identity: all primary key values are unique and no part of the primary key is null
Every foreign key matches a primary key
Every table has at least one row
Every column has a data type
questions.explanation: Example: no invoice can have a duplicate number, nor can it be null.

questions.question: What is referential integrity?
options: Every table has a primary key
Every reference to a record in one table by a record in a related table is valid (no orphaned records)
Every primary key is an integer
No two tables have the same column name
questions.explanation: A foreign key may have either a null entry or one value matching a primary key in the related table.

questions.question: A customer has not yet been assigned a sales representative. Which statement about the foreign key rep_number in CUSTOMER is true?
options: It must hold a valid rep number; null is never allowed
It may hold any number
It may be null, but it cannot hold a rep number that doesn't exist in the sales representative table
It must be deleted from the table
questions.explanation: It is possible for an attribute to have no corresponding value, but impossible to have an invalid entry.

questions.question: With referential integrity enforced, what happens if you try to delete a row whose primary key has matching foreign key values in another table?
options: The matching rows are silently ignored
The database creates a new primary key
The primary key becomes null
The deletion is not allowed
questions.explanation: Enforcing it makes it impossible to delete a row in one table whose primary key has mandatory matching foreign key values in another.

questions.question: What is null?
options: The absence of any data value (unknown, known but missing, or inapplicable)
The number zero
An empty string
The word NULL typed as text
questions.explanation: Null is not zero and not a blank.

questions.question: A primary key may contain a null value as long as the remaining values are unique.
questions.explanation: Entity integrity forbids null in any part of the primary key.

questions.question: Match each term to its description.

pairs.right: A description of all tables in the database, created by the user and designer
The complete logical view of the database
Primary key values are unique and never null
A foreign key is either null or matches a primary key in the related table

questions.question: Match each relationship type to its description.

pairs.right: The norm for relational databases; the most common type
One entity can be related to only one other entity
Implemented by creating a new connecting entity in 1:M relationships with the original entities

questions.question: A composite (bridge or associative) entity that resolves an M:N relationship contains:
options: Only a new surrogate key
The primary keys of the tables to be linked, as foreign keys
A copy of every attribute from both tables
Nothing; it is an empty table
questions.explanation: In Harborview, the gadget_group_map table is a bridge that links gadget and gadget_group.

questions.question: Chen notation allows direct representation of M:N relationships.
questions.explanation: Crow's Foot notation does not; it needs a bridge table (associative entity).

questions.question: Crow's Foot notation allows direct representation of M:N relationships.
questions.explanation: Crow's Foot needs a bridge table (associative entity). Chen notation can show M:N directly.

questions.question: Summary of the relational model: which statement is correct?
options: Keys are optional in relational tables
Rows are the basic building blocks and tables are optional
Tables are the basic building blocks, keys are central to their use, and each table row must have a primary key
Tables can only be linked through the data dictionary
questions.explanation: Although the tables are independent, they are linked by common attributes (foreign keys).

questions.question: What is normalization?
options: Converting all data to the same format
Adding indexes to speed up queries
Encrypting the tables
Evaluating and correcting table structures to minimize data redundancies
questions.explanation: It reduces data anomalies and assigns attributes to tables based on determination.

questions.question: Match each normal form to its characteristic.

pairs.right: Table format, no repeating groups, and the primary key is identified
1NF and no partial dependencies
2NF and no transitive dependencies

questions.question: A table is in 2NF when:
options: It is in 1NF and has no partial dependencies
It is in 1NF and has no transitive dependencies
It has no primary key
It has only one column
questions.explanation: If a 1NF table has a single-attribute primary key, it is automatically in 2NF.

questions.question: A table is in 3NF when:
options: It is in 1NF and has no partial dependencies
It is in 2NF and has no transitive dependencies
It has no foreign keys
It has at most three columns
questions.explanation: Convert 2NF to 3NF by making new tables to eliminate transitive dependencies and reassigning the dependent attributes.

questions.question: What is a functional dependence?
options: Two attributes that always have the same data type
An attribute that cannot be null
Attribute B is functionally dependent on attribute A if each value of A determines one and only one value of B
A column that references another table
questions.explanation: Written A → B, where A is the determinant and B is the dependent attribute. Example: PROJ_NUM → PROJ_NAME.

questions.question: What is a partial dependency?
options: A dependency of one non-key attribute on another non-key attribute
A dependency on the whole primary key
A dependency that holds for only some rows
A functional dependence in which the determinant is only part of the primary key
questions.explanation: A necessary condition is a composite primary key. Partial dependencies are removed to reach 2NF.

questions.question: What is a transitive dependency?
options: An attribute that depends on another non-primary-key attribute
An attribute that depends on only part of the primary key
An attribute that depends on the whole primary key
A dependency that crosses two tables
questions.explanation: It occurs only when a functional dependence exists among non-key attributes, and it is more difficult to identify. Transitive dependencies are removed to reach 3NF.

questions.question: A table has the primary key (proj_num, emp_num) and the dependency proj_num → proj_name. What kind of dependency is that?
options: A transitive dependency
A partial dependency
A full functional dependency
A multivalued dependency
questions.explanation: The determinant, proj_num, is only part of the composite primary key.

questions.question: In the same table, emp_num → job_class and job_class → chg_hour. What kind of dependency is job_class → chg_hour?
options: A partial dependency
A dependency on the whole key
A transitive dependency
A referential dependency
questions.explanation: chg_hour depends on job_class, which is not part of the primary key.

questions.question: A table has the primary key (proj_num, emp_num) and the dependency (proj_num, emp_num) → assign_hours. What kind of dependency is it?
options: A partial dependency
A transitive dependency
No dependency
A full functional dependency on the whole primary key
questions.explanation: assign_hours depends on the entire composite key, and not on any subset of it.

questions.question: The four dependencies are: proj_num → proj_name; emp_num → emp_name, job_class; job_class → chg_hour; proj_num, emp_num → assign_hours. Which set of 3NF tables results?
options: PROJECT(proj_num, proj_name), EMPLOYEE(emp_num, emp_name, job_class), JOB(job_class, chg_hour), ASSIGNMENT(proj_num, emp_num, assign_hours)
One table with all six attributes
PROJECT(proj_num, proj_name) and ASSIGNMENT(proj_num, emp_num, emp_name, job_class, chg_hour, assign_hours)
EMPLOYEE(emp_num, emp_name, job_class, chg_hour) and ASSIGNMENT(proj_num, emp_num, assign_hours)
questions.explanation: Each determinant becomes the primary key of its own table, which removes the partial dependencies (for 2NF) and the transitive dependency job_class → chg_hour (for 3NF).

questions.question: Which of these describes 1NF?
options: A table with no partial dependencies
A tabular format in which all key attributes are defined, there are no repeating groups, and all attributes depend on the primary key
A table with no transitive dependencies
A table with exactly one column
questions.explanation: All relational tables satisfy 1NF requirements.

questions.question: A table cannot be a valid relational table without already being in 1NF.
questions.explanation: All relational tables satisfy the 1NF requirements.

questions.question: How do you convert a table to 2NF?
options: Remove all foreign keys
Add a surrogate key to every table
Make new tables to eliminate the partial dependencies and reassign the dependent attributes to them
Merge the tables back together
questions.explanation: Remove the composite primary key from the 1NF table, creating tables for each determinant that is part of it.

questions.question: What is denormalization?
options: Producing a higher normal form
Deleting all of the foreign keys
Removing the primary keys
Producing a lower normal form, which results in increased performance and greater data redundancy
questions.explanation: It is sometimes necessary.

questions.question: Why is denormalization sometimes necessary?
options: Joining a large number of tables takes additional I/O operations and processing logic, which reduces system speed
Because normalized tables cannot be queried
Because 3NF tables have no keys
Because denormalized tables use less storage
questions.explanation: Design goals include both normalized relations and processing requirements and speed.

questions.question: Denormalization increases data redundancy in exchange for faster processing.
questions.explanation: Fewer joins means faster queries, but redundancy is back, so the application must keep the copies consistent.

questions.question: Match each category of SQL to its commands.

pairs.right: CREATE TABLE/DATABASE, DROP TABLE/DATABASE, ALTER TABLE
INSERT, SELECT, UPDATE, DELETE (CRUD)
COMMIT, ROLLBACK
GRANT, REVOKE

questions.question: What does CRUD stand for in SQL's data manipulation language?
options: Create, Retrieve, Use, Drop
Create (INSERT), Read (SELECT), Update (UPDATE), Delete (DELETE)
Commit, Rollback, Update, Define
Copy, Remove, Undo, Display
questions.explanation: These four commands are the DML.

questions.question: Match each DDL command to what it does.

pairs.right: Creates the database schema
Removes the database schema entirely
Creates a new table
Modifies a table's definition (add, modify or delete attributes or constraints)
Permanently deletes a table and its data

questions.question: Which command changes a table's structure, such as adding a column?
options: UPDATE
CREATE VIEW
ALTER TABLE
DROP TABLE
questions.explanation: UPDATE changes the data in rows, not the structure.

questions.question: Which of these is a DDL command?
options: INSERT
SELECT
UPDATE
CREATE TABLE
questions.explanation: INSERT, SELECT and UPDATE are DML.

questions.question: What does the DISTINCT keyword do in a SELECT?
options: Produces a list of only unique values
Sorts the result in ascending order
Returns only the first row
Removes null values
questions.explanation: For example: `SELECT DISTINCT v_code FROM product;`

questions.question: Which clause of a SELECT statement specifies the table or tables from which the data is retrieved?
options: WHERE
FROM
GROUP BY
SELECT
questions.explanation: SELECT lists the columns, FROM names the tables.

questions.question: Which syntax joins two tables on a column with the same name in both?
options: SELECT column-list FROM table1 JOIN table2 WHERE common_column
SELECT column-list FROM table1, table2 GROUP BY common_column
SELECT column-list FROM table1 JOIN table2 USING (common_column)
SELECT column-list FROM table1 UNION table2
questions.explanation: The USING column must exist in both tables, and only rows with matching values are returned.

questions.question: When should JOIN ... ON be used instead of JOIN ... USING?
options: When you need an outer join only
When both tables are the same
ON can only be used with three tables
When the tables do not share a common column name, so you express the join condition explicitly
questions.explanation: Syntax: `SELECT column-list FROM table1 JOIN table2 ON join-condition`.

questions.question: What is a recursive join?
options: A join of a table to itself
A join of more than three tables
A join that returns every row
A join without a condition
questions.explanation: A recursive query joins a table to itself, for example an employee to their supervisor.

questions.question: Which clause sorts the final result of a query?
options: GROUP BY
ORDER BY
HAVING
DISTINCT
questions.explanation: `ORDER BY last_name, first_name` sorts first by last name, then by first name; DESC reverses a column's order.

questions.question: What does the WHERE clause do?
options: Sorts the rows
Groups the rows
Adds conditional restrictions to the SELECT statement to limit the rows returned
Names the tables to use
questions.explanation: WHERE is also used with UPDATE and DELETE to restrict the rows affected.

questions.question: Match each special operator to its use.

pairs.right: Checks whether a value falls within a range
Checks whether a value matches any value in a list
Matches a pattern, using wildcards such as %

questions.question: Which rows does `WHERE last_name LIKE 'R%'` return?
options: Rows whose last_name ends with R
Rows whose last_name is exactly R
Rows whose last_name contains an R anywhere
Rows whose last_name starts with R
questions.explanation: `%` matches any number of characters. `'%R'` would be ends with R, and `'%R%'` contains R.

questions.question: Which clause shows only the groups produced by GROUP BY that meet a condition?
options: HAVING
WHERE
ORDER BY
DISTINCT
questions.explanation: HAVING operates like WHERE, but is applied to the output of the GROUP BY operation.

questions.question: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING?
options: WHERE filters groups; HAVING filters rows
WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters the groups after GROUP BY
They are identical
HAVING can be used only without GROUP BY
questions.explanation: A condition on an aggregate such as COUNT(*) >= 10 belongs in HAVING.

questions.question: Match each aggregate function to what it computes.

pairs.right: The number of rows
The smallest value
The largest value
The total of the values
The average of the values

questions.question: In what order are the clauses of a SELECT written?
options: SELECT, WHERE, FROM, ORDER BY, GROUP BY, HAVING
FROM, SELECT, WHERE, HAVING, GROUP BY, ORDER BY
SELECT, FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY
SELECT, FROM, GROUP BY, WHERE, ORDER BY, HAVING
questions.explanation: Build one clause at a time in this order; WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING and ORDER BY are optional.

questions.question: Which statement adds new rows to a table?
options: UPDATE
ALTER
SELECT
INSERT
questions.explanation: `INSERT INTO tablename (field1, field2) VALUES (value1, value2);` Each value must be in the same order as the field names.

questions.question: Which statement modifies existing rows?
options: UPDATE
INSERT
ALTER
DELETE
questions.explanation: `UPDATE tablename SET column = expression [WHERE condition];` Always use WHERE to specify which rows.

questions.question: Which statement gets rid of rows?
options: DROP
DELETE
REMOVE
UPDATE
questions.explanation: `DELETE FROM tablename [WHERE condition];` Always use WHERE to limit the damage.

questions.question: What happens if you run an UPDATE or DELETE with no WHERE clause?
options: Nothing happens
Only the first row is affected
Every row in the table is affected
The statement is rejected as a syntax error
questions.explanation: That is why the rule is: always use WHERE to specify which rows.

questions.question: What is a view?
options: A copy of a table stored on disk
A backup of the schema
An index on a primary key
A virtual table based on a SELECT query
questions.explanation: `CREATE VIEW viewname AS SELECT query` is a DDL command that stores the subquery in the data dictionary. The tables it is based on are the base tables.

questions.question: SQL essentially has two sets of commands:
options: Data definition language (DDL) and data manipulation language (DML)
Queries and reports
Tables and views
Keys and indexes
questions.explanation: DDL defines the structure and DML works with the data.

questions.question: Table joins are classified as:
options: Primary joins and foreign joins
Inner joins and outer joins
Natural joins and artificial joins only
Left joins and up joins
questions.explanation: Joins use keywords like USING and ON. An inner join returns only rows that match on a common value; an outer join also returns unmatched rows.

questions.question: Which of these are ANSI standard SQL data types?
options: TABLE, ROW, COLUMN and KEY
SELECT, FROM and WHERE
DECIMAL, INTEGER, FLOAT, CHAR, VARCHAR, DATE and DATETIME
PRIMARY, FOREIGN and UNIQUE
questions.explanation: They are supported by all RDBMS vendors in different ways.

questions.question: Select all fields and all records from the region table.
questions.solution: SELECT * FROM region;
questions.explanation: The asterisk is a wildcard for 'every column'.

questions.question: Select just the gadget_title and daily_fee fields from every record in the gadget table.
questions.solution: SELECT gadget_title, daily_fee FROM gadget;
questions.explanation: List the columns, separated by commas, then name the table.

questions.question: Select the gadget_title of every gadget whose daily_fee is above 10.
questions.solution: SELECT gadget_title FROM gadget WHERE daily_fee > 10;
questions.explanation: WHERE restricts the rows returned.

questions.question: Select the total amount in the ledger_entry table for the patron with patron_id = 8.
questions.solution: SELECT SUM(amount) FROM ledger_entry WHERE patron_id = 8;
questions.explanation: SUM is an aggregate: it reduces the matching rows to a single value.

questions.question: Select the total amount recorded by the steward with steward_id = 2, rounded to the nearest whole number.
questions.solution: SELECT ROUND(SUM(amount)) FROM ledger_entry WHERE steward_id = 2;
questions.explanation: ROUND wraps the aggregate.

questions.question: List the gadget_title of all gadgets in the group labelled 'Plumbing'. (Join gadget, gadget_group_map and gadget_group.)
questions.solution:
SELECT gadget_title FROM gadget
  JOIN gadget_group_map USING (gadget_id)
  JOIN gadget_group USING (group_id)
WHERE group_label = 'Plumbing';
questions.explanation: Chain the joins through the bridge table using USING on the shared key names.

questions.question: List the titles of all gadgets with the word drill in the gadget_title.
questions.solution: SELECT gadget_title FROM gadget WHERE gadget_title LIKE '%drill%';
questions.explanation: % on both sides matches the word anywhere in the title.

questions.question: List the contact_email of all patrons whose given_name ends in in.
questions.solution: SELECT contact_email FROM patron WHERE given_name LIKE '%in';
questions.explanation: '%in' means anything followed by 'in'.

questions.question: How many times did the patron with patron_id = 34 check out a unit in the month of June (any year)? Use the MONTH() function on checked_out_on.
questions.solution: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM checkout WHERE patron_id = 34 AND MONTH(checked_out_on) = 6;
questions.explanation: MONTH(date) returns the numeric month of the date passed to it.

questions.question: Select all fields from the maker table where the maker_name includes the letters TOOL, matching any case, using UPPER().
questions.solution: SELECT * FROM maker WHERE UPPER(maker_name) LIKE '%TOOL%';
questions.explanation: Converting to upper case first makes the match case-insensitive.

questions.question: List the maker_name and home_region of the makers whose home_region is either Canada or Italy, using IN.
questions.solution: SELECT maker_name, home_region FROM maker WHERE home_region IN ('Canada', 'Italy');
questions.explanation: IN is a shorter way of writing several OR conditions.

questions.question: List the maker_name and home_region of the makers whose home_region is either Canada or Italy, using OR instead of IN.
questions.solution: SELECT maker_name, home_region FROM maker WHERE home_region = 'Canada' OR home_region = 'Italy';
questions.explanation: Both forms return the same rows.

questions.question: Select checkout_id, checked_out_on, unit_id and patron_id from the checkout table for checkouts between '2024-06-01' and '2024-06-15'. Use BETWEEN ... AND ...
questions.solution:
SELECT checkout_id, checked_out_on, unit_id, patron_id FROM checkout
WHERE checked_out_on BETWEEN '2024-06-01' AND '2024-06-15';
questions.explanation: Dates use the YYYY-MM-DD format. BETWEEN includes both end values.

questions.question: List the first and last names of patrons who checked out a unit between '2024-06-01' and '2024-06-30', each patron once, ordered by surname. Use DISTINCT.
questions.solution:
SELECT DISTINCT given_name, surname FROM checkout
  JOIN patron USING (patron_id)
WHERE checked_out_on BETWEEN '2024-06-01' AND '2024-06-30'
ORDER BY surname;
questions.explanation: DISTINCT removes the duplicates from patrons who borrowed more than once.

questions.question: List each steward's surname alongside their supervisor's surname (stewards with no supervisor can be left out). This is a recursive join; join steward to itself using aliases.
questions.explanation: A table alias identifies which copy of the table each column came from. The join condition uses ON because the columns have different names.

questions.question: List all patrons' given_name and surname, sorted by surname and then by given_name.
questions.solution: SELECT given_name, surname FROM patron ORDER BY surname, given_name;
questions.explanation: A cascading order sequence sorts by the first column, then the second within ties.

questions.question: List each gadget_title and daily_fee, with the most expensive daily_fee first.
questions.solution: SELECT gadget_title, daily_fee FROM gadget ORDER BY daily_fee DESC;
questions.explanation: DESC reverses the sort.

questions.question: List each different power_source in the gadget table once.
questions.solution: SELECT DISTINCT power_source FROM gadget;
questions.explanation: DISTINCT removes duplicate values.

questions.question: Show the lowest, highest and average daily_fee in the gadget table.
questions.solution: SELECT MIN(daily_fee), MAX(daily_fee), AVG(daily_fee) FROM gadget;
questions.explanation: Each aggregate reduces the whole table to one value.

questions.question: How many checkouts were made in each year? Show the year and the count, grouped by year.
questions.explanation: GROUP BY collects the rows sharing the same value so that the aggregate is computed per group.

questions.question: How many gadgets are there for each power_source? Show the power_source and the count.
questions.solution: SELECT power_source, COUNT(*) AS gadgets FROM gadget GROUP BY power_source;
questions.explanation: One output row per group.

questions.question: Summarize the number of checkouts per patron, limited to the patrons with 10 or more checkouts. Show patron_id and the count.
questions.solution:
SELECT patron_id, COUNT(*) AS num_checkouts
FROM checkout
GROUP BY patron_id
HAVING num_checkouts >= 10;
questions.explanation: The condition is on an aggregate, so it must be in HAVING, not WHERE.

questions.question: Show the number of checkouts in each month of 2025. Show the month number and the count.
questions.solution:
SELECT MONTH(checked_out_on) AS checkout_month, COUNT(*) AS number_of_checkouts
FROM checkout
WHERE YEAR(checked_out_on) = 2025
GROUP BY checkout_month;
questions.explanation: WHERE restricts the rows to 2025 before they are grouped.

questions.question: Add a new row to gadget_group with group_id 12 and group_label 'Concrete and Masonry'.
questions.solution:
INSERT INTO gadget_group (group_id, group_label)
VALUES (12, 'Concrete and Masonry');
questions.verify: SELECT group_id, group_label FROM gadget_group ORDER BY group_id
questions.explanation: The values are in the same order as the column names. Graded on the table afterwards.

questions.question: Change the daily_fee of the gadget with gadget_id = 1 to 12.50.
questions.solution: UPDATE gadget SET daily_fee = 12.50 WHERE gadget_id = 1;
questions.verify: SELECT gadget_id, daily_fee FROM gadget ORDER BY gadget_id
questions.explanation: Always use WHERE to say which rows to change; without it every gadget would be updated.

questions.question: Delete every row for group_id 8 from the gadget_group_map table.
questions.solution: DELETE FROM gadget_group_map WHERE group_id = 8;
questions.verify: SELECT gadget_id, group_id FROM gadget_group_map ORDER BY gadget_id, group_id
questions.explanation: Referential integrity means the child rows in the bridge table have to go before the parent row. Always use WHERE to limit the damage.

questions.question: You run `UPDATE gadget SET daily_fee = 5;` with no WHERE clause. What happens?
options: Only the first gadget is changed
Nothing; SQL requires a WHERE clause
Only gadgets with a fee are changed
Every gadget's daily_fee is set to 5
questions.explanation: The reason to always use WHERE with UPDATE and DELETE.

questions.question: What is a transaction?
options: A sequence of database operations that access or modify the database as a unit
Any SELECT statement
A single UPDATE of a single row only
A purchase made by a customer
questions.explanation: A transaction is all or nothing.

questions.question: The four properties of a transaction are summarized by the acronym ______.
questions.explanation: Atomic, Consistent, Isolated, Durable.

questions.question: Match each ACID property to its meaning.

pairs.right: Either all of the transaction's operations happen or none of them do
The database moves from one valid state to another
Concurrent transactions do not interfere with one another
Once committed, the changes persist, even after a failure

questions.question: Which two TCL commands does SQL provide for transactions?
options: GRANT and REVOKE
COMMIT and ROLLBACK
INSERT and DELETE
SAVE and LOAD
questions.explanation: COMMIT saves the changes to disk; ROLLBACK restores the previous database state.

questions.question: What does COMMIT do?
options: Undoes the changes
Locks every table
Saves the changes made by the transaction to disk
Starts a new transaction without saving
questions.explanation: Changes made before the commit can still be rolled back.

questions.question: What does ROLLBACK do?
options: Saves the changes permanently
Deletes the table
Shows what changes were made
Restores the database to its previous state
questions.explanation: It undoes the transaction's uncommitted changes.

questions.question: What is concurrency control?
options: Coordinating the simultaneous execution of transactions
Limiting the number of tables
Copying data to another server
Encrypting database traffic
questions.explanation: Multiple users must be able to use the database at the same time without compromising integrity.

questions.question: What do locks do?
options: Prevent anyone from ever reading data
Guarantee a transaction unique access to a data item
Encrypt the data item
Make a table read-only forever
questions.explanation: Locks can result in deadlock.

questions.question: What is a deadlock (a 'deadly embrace')?
options: A table that cannot be opened
A transaction that was rolled back
Two users each want the data the other has locked
A lock that expires after one second
questions.explanation: Each transaction waits for the other to release its lock, so neither can proceed.

questions.question: Which statement about optimistic concurrency control is correct?
options: It locks every row before each transaction
It requires all transactions to run one at a time
It assumes that most transactions conflict
It assumes the majority of transactions do not conflict, and executes them concurrently using private, temporary copies of data
questions.explanation: Time stamping is an example of an optimistic method: each transaction gets a unique time stamp, and conflicting transactions are scheduled in time stamp order.

questions.question: Concurrency control with time stamping is an optimistic method.
questions.explanation: Time stamping assigns each transaction a unique time stamp and schedules conflicting transactions in time stamp order.

questions.question: Why is operational data not well suited for decision support?
options: It is optimized for updates, modifications and inserts (highly normalized, minimal storage, many joins) rather than for reading and analysis
It is stored in spreadsheets
It is always unstructured
It does not contain historical data of any kind
questions.explanation: Operational data is highly normalized; a data warehouse is denormalized and optimized for reading speed.

questions.question: Which statement describes a data warehouse?
options: A highly normalized database optimized for updates
An integrated, subject-oriented, time-variant, nonvolatile collection of data that supports decision making; denormalized and optimized for reading speed
A temporary table for one report
A collection of unrelated spreadsheets
questions.explanation: It is optimized for read speed, not for space and storage.

questions.question: What is Big Data?
options: Any database with more than 100 tables
Data stored in the cloud
Data of such volume, velocity and variety that the relational model struggles to adapt to it
Data that is highly normalized
questions.explanation: Volume, velocity and variety are collectively called the 3 Vs of Big Data.

questions.question: Match each of the 3 Vs of Big Data to its meaning.

pairs.right: The sheer amount of data
The speed at which data is generated and must be processed
The many different forms the data takes

questions.question: What is Hadoop?
options: A query language
A relational DBMS
A kind of ERD
The framework that emerged as the standard for the physical storage of Big Data
questions.explanation: It was quickly adopted for Big Data storage.

questions.question: What does NoSQL mean?
options: A broad term for several nonrelational database approaches to data management
Any database that does not use a network
A database with no data
A SQL dialect without SELECT
questions.explanation: The main types include key-value, document, column-oriented and graph databases.

questions.question: What is a key-value database?
options: A database with only two tables
A database that stores data in key-value pairs, where the key is the primary key
A relational database with a surrogate key
A database that stores only keys
questions.explanation: Example value: "name John, age 31, city New York".

questions.question: How does a document database differ from a key-value database?
options: It has no keys
It stores data in tables with foreign keys
The value component is an encoded document, such as JSON
It stores only PDF files
questions.explanation: Example document: {name: "John", age: 31, city: "New York"}.

questions.question: What is MongoDB?
options: A graph database that stores nodes and edges
A relational database
A Big Data framework for physical storage
A document (NoSQL) database that stores documents in JSON format
questions.explanation: Neo4j is the graph database example.

questions.question: What is database connectivity?
options: The mechanisms through which applications connect and communicate with data repositories
The speed of a network connection
A kind of foreign key
Copying data between tables
questions.explanation: Examples include ODBC, native connectivity and OLE-DB.

questions.question: Which database connectivity interface is the most popular and common?
options: Object Linking and Embedding for Databases (OLE-DB)
Open Database Connectivity (ODBC)
Native database connectivity
Extensible Markup Language (XML)
questions.explanation: ODBC is most popular and common.

questions.question: What is cloud computing?
options: Running software only on a local server
A way of encrypting databases
A computing model that provides ubiquitous, on-demand access to a shared pool of configurable resources that can be rapidly provisioned
A type of query language
questions.explanation: AWS, Azure and Google Cloud are examples of providers.
